method: symmetric four-world authoring, post-hoc seeded key selection

worlds.line: Your back pay went through on last night's payroll run.
worlds.reply: I'll stop checking the balance now — that's been weeks.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The line reports that money already owed has now been paid. Standing down from the daily balance-watching is exactly what someone does when the payment they were waiting for has landed. The reply promising to get a supervisor to authorize the hours and resubmit treats a completed payment as a refused one; the reply nominating a credit union account answers a routing question nobody asked; and the reply apologizing for leaving an ID bag downstairs responds to an identity check the line never requests.

kills.1: The line says the money "went through" already, so promising to have the hours authorized and resubmitted treats a completed payment as a rejection.
kills.2: "went through on last night's payroll run" reports where the money has already landed, so naming an account to pay it into answers a question that was never posed.
kills.3: "Your back pay" is described as paid, not as held pending identification, so promising to fetch an ID from a bag downstairs meets a demand the line does not make.

worlds.line: Payroll rejected the claim; your hours weren't authorized.
worlds.reply: Okay — I'll get my supervisor to authorize them and resubmit.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The line delivers a refusal and names its cause: the hours lacked authorization. Undertaking to obtain that authorization and send the claim again addresses precisely the stated obstacle. The reply announcing an end to balance-checking celebrates a deposit that did not happen; the reply naming a credit union account picks a destination for money that is not being paid; and the reply about an ID in a bag downstairs fixes the wrong blocker, since identity was never the problem.

kills.0: "rejected the claim" means nothing was deposited, so saying you will stop checking the balance treats a refusal as a payment.
kills.2: "your hours weren't authorized" is a reason for non-payment, so choosing which account should receive the money assumes a payment the line has just denied.
kills.3: The named obstacle is that "your hours weren't authorized", not that you are unidentified, so producing an ID card addresses something the line rules out.

worlds.line: Which account do you want the missing week paid into?
worlds.reply: The credit union one — I'll write the number down for you.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The line asks the payee to choose a destination for a payment that is going ahead. Naming the account and offering to write the details out is the cooperative answer. The reply announcing an end to balance-checking leaves the clerk without the information just asked for; the reply about getting hours authorized and resubmitting contradicts the line's premise that the money is being paid; and the reply about an ID in a bag downstairs offers proof of identity when the question was about banking details.

kills.0: "Which account do you want" is a direct question, so replying that you will stop checking the balance leaves the clerk without the answer needed to pay you.
kills.1: The line takes for granted that "the missing week" is going to be paid, so proposing to get the hours authorized and resubmit contradicts its premise.
kills.3: "Which account" asks about a bank destination, so promising to fetch an ID card supplies the wrong kind of information entirely.

worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The line makes an identity check a precondition before anything else happens. Saying the card is close by and asking for a moment is straightforward compliance. The reply that stops the daily balance-checking treats the matter as finished when a step is still outstanding; the reply about authorizing hours and resubmitting responds to a rejection that was not announced; and the reply naming a credit union account volunteers banking details when what was asked for was proof of identity.

kills.1: "Come back with your ID card" is a request for a document, not news of a refusal, so promising a resubmission answers something the line never said.
kills.2: "so I can verify you" is about proving who you are, so volunteering a bank account does not satisfy what the line asks for.
